card.name: Sweeping 'every' and 'all' in old prose
card.fires_on: Words of totality or extent such as 'every', 'all' and 'extend' in formal, old-fashioned historical or biographical prose. The word comes just before a noun like sort, part, variety or history.

modes.label: Every/all before a noun
modes.description: 'every' or 'all' introduces a broad sweep of things in a long literary sentence.
modes.example: though filled with<< every>> sort of detail regarding missionary life and work

modes.label: Extend to
modes.description: The verb 'extend' leads into a phrase meaning everywhere.
modes.example: or as an existing power whose influence and activity<< extend>> to every part of the globe.

card.writes: It pushes toward words like 'feature' and 'features', but the effect is weak and mixed.
card.plain: It marks sweeping words like 'every' or 'all' in dated, formal historical writing.
